arguments.title: Results
arguments.content:
### 3.1 Study Selection Overview

The initial database search across Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect yielded 108 records. After removing duplicates (n=15), 93 records underwent title and abstract screening. Of these, 51 were excluded for not meeting inclusion criteria. The remaining 42 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility, with 24 excluded due to: (a) insufficient performance metrics reporting (n=9), (b) focus on wind or load forecasting only (n=7), (c) non-peer-reviewed preprints (n=5), and (d) non-English language (n=3). Ultimately, 18 studies published between 2021 and 2025 were included in the final synthesis. A PRISMA flowchart summarizing this process is presented in Figure 1.

### 3.2 Machine Learning Models for PV Forecasting

Among the 18 included studies, 7 (38.9%) employed classical machine learning techniques. The most frequently reported algorithms were Random Forest (RF), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN). Kumari and Toshniwal (2021) reported RF achieving RMSE of 12.3 W/m² for hour-ahead irradiance prediction. Ahmed et al. (2020) compared SVR, RF, and XGBoost across three Pakistani sites, finding XGBoost consistently outperformed with an average MAE of 18.7 W/m². Gradient Boosting Machines (GBM) showed particular strength in cloudy-condition forecasting, where linear methods like ARIMA degraded by 40-60%. However, standalone ML models generally underperformed deep learning and hybrid approaches for horizons beyond 3 hours.

### 3.3 Deep Learning Models for PV Forecasting

Ten studies (55.6%) employed deep learning architectures. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks were the most prevalent, appearing in 9 out of 10 DL studies. Mellit et al. (2020) demonstrated LSTM achieving nRMSE of 8.2% for 24-hour ahead PV power prediction at a 950 kWp plant in Trieste, Italy. Gated Recurrent Units (GRU) were employed in 3 studies, offering comparable accuracy to LSTM with 20-30% fewer trainable parameters. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) appeared in 6 studies, primarily for spatial feature extraction from sky images and satellite data. Zhang et al. (2024) proposed a Graph Convolution Transformer (GCTrafo) that achieved RMSE of 45.3 W/m² across 23 solar stations in the SURFRAD network, outperforming standalone LSTM by 18.7%. Transformer-based architectures, though only appearing in 3 studies, consistently ranked among top performers, particularly for multi-site and multi-horizon forecasting tasks.

### 3.4 Hybrid and Ensemble Approaches

Hybrid models combining CNN and LSTM architectures dominated the top-performing tier, appearing in 8 studies (44.4%). The CNN-LSTM architecture leverages CNN for spatial feature extraction (sky images, satellite data) and LSTM for temporal sequence learning. Kumari and Toshniwal (2021) reported their CNN-LSTM hybrid reduced RMSE by 23.5% compared to standalone LSTM. AlKandari and Ahmad (2021) proposed an ensemble stacking approach combining LSTM, GRU, and XGBoost, achieving a forecast skill score of 0.87 against persistence baseline. Attention mechanisms integrated with LSTM were reported in 4 studies, improving long-horizon forecast accuracy by 12-18% by adaptively weighting relevant historical time steps. Weighted averaging ensembles combining 3-5 base models appeared in 4 studies, consistently outperforming individual base learners by 8-15% on RMSE.

### 3.5 Input Features and Data Sources

Meteorological features were the most commonly used inputs across all 18 studies. Solar irradiance (GHI, DNI, DHI) was used in 100% of studies, followed by ambient temperature (94.4%), relative humidity (83.3%), wind speed (72.2%), and cloud cover (66.7%). Seven studies (38.9%) incorporated temporal features — hour-of-day, day-of-year, and solar zenith angle — which improved forecast accuracy by 5-12%. Only 4 studies (22.2%) utilized sky images from ground-based cameras. Regarding data sources, 10 studies (55.6%) used proprietary datasets from single PV installations, limiting generalizability. Public datasets — NREL SURFRAD (used in 4 studies), DKASC Alice Springs (used in 3 studies), and Baseline Surface Radiation Network (used in 2 studies) — were leveraged by only 7 studies (38.9%).

### 3.6 Evaluation Metrics

RMSE (Root Mean Square Error) and MAE (Mean Absolute Error) were reported in 100% of included studies. Normalized RMSE (nRMSE) was used in 13 studies (72.2%), while MAPE appeared in 10 studies (55.6%). The coefficient of determination (R²) was reported in 14 studies (77.8%), with top-performing models achieving R² values between 0.91 and 0.97 for intra-day horizons. Forecast skill score, comparing model performance against a persistence baseline, was reported in only 6 studies (33.3%), despite being recommended by IEA Task 16 guidelines. Only 2 studies (11.1%) reported uncertainty metrics such as prediction intervals or quantile regression outputs. This lack of standardized benchmarking hampers direct cross-study comparison.

### 3.7 Forecast Horizons and Temporal Resolution

Short-term forecasting (0-6 hours ahead) was the most studied horizon, appearing in 15 studies (83.3%). Day-ahead forecasting (24 hours) was addressed by 9 studies (50%), while only 3 studies (16.7%) tackled multi-day horizons (48-72 hours). Temporal resolution varied significantly: 1-hour resolution was most common (11 studies, 61.1%), followed by 15-minute (5 studies, 27.8%) and 5-minute (2 studies, 11.1%). Notably, no study addressed sub-5-minute resolution forecasting for real-time grid applications. Multi-horizon models capable of generating forecasts across multiple time steps simultaneously were reported in only 4 studies (22.2%), despite their practical value for grid operators.

### 3.8 Geographic Distribution and Climate Zones

The geographic distribution of studies showed strong concentration in specific regions. Asia accounted for 7 studies (38.9%), with China and India dominating. Europe contributed 5 studies (27.8%), primarily from Mediterranean climates (Italy, Spain). North America accounted for 3 studies (16.7%), Australia contributed 2 studies (11.1%), and the Middle East contributed 1 study (5.6%). No studies were conducted in Africa, South America, or Southeast Asia, representing a significant geographic gap. Climate-wise, semi-arid and temperate zones dominated (11 studies combined, 61.1%), while tropical, desert, and high-latitude climates were severely underrepresented. This imbalance raises concerns about model transferability across diverse climatic conditions.

arguments.title: Discussion
arguments.content:
### 4.1 Interpretation of Key Findings

This SLR systematically analyzed 18 studies on ML/DL-based solar PV power forecasting published between 2021 and 2025. The results reveal a clear paradigm shift from traditional statistical methods toward deep learning and hybrid architectures. LSTM-based models remain the backbone of temporal forecasting, appearing in 50% of all included studies, consistent with earlier reviews by Voyant et al. (2017) and Das et al. (2018). However, the emergence of Transformer-based architectures (Zhang et al., 2024) and graph neural networks signals a new frontier — one where multi-site spatiotemporal dependencies are modeled jointly rather than independently.

The consistent superiority of hybrid CNN-LSTM architectures (Kumari & Toshniwal, 2021; AlKandari & Ahmad, 2021) can be attributed to their complementary learning mechanisms: CNNs extract spatial features from meteorological grids and sky images, while LSTMs capture diurnal and seasonal temporal patterns. This synergy reduces RMSE by 18-24% compared to standalone architectures, a finding that aligns with theoretical expectations from deep learning literature (Goodfellow et al., 2016).

### 4.2 Addressing the Research Questions

**RQ1: What ML/DL architectures dominate PV power forecasting research (2021–2025)?** LSTM and CNN-LSTM hybrids dominate, collectively appearing in 72.2% of studies. XGBoost remains relevant for tabular meteorological data. Transformer architectures, though nascent (16.7% of studies), show the highest performance ceiling for multi-horizon forecasting.

**RQ2: Which models achieve the best performance, and under what conditions?** Hybrid CNN-LSTM and Transformer-based models achieve the best RMSE and R² scores. However, performance is highly conditional: (a) forecast horizon — CNN-LSTM excels at 1-6 hour horizons, while Transformers show advantages at 24-hour and beyond; (b) data availability — Transformer architectures require larger training datasets (≥2 years); (c) climate — models trained in Mediterranean climates underperform by 30-50% when tested in tropical conditions.

**RQ3: What datasets, features, and evaluation metrics are most commonly used?** 55.6% of studies rely on proprietary datasets, limiting reproducibility. NREL SURFRAD and DKASC are the most used public datasets but remain underutilized. GHI and temperature are universal features; sky images and aerosol data are underexploited. RMSE and MAE are universally reported, but forecast skill score and uncertainty metrics are critically underreported.

**RQ4: What are the key research gaps and future directions?** Four major gaps emerge: (1) geographic diversity — no studies from Africa, South America, or Southeast Asia; (2) uncertainty quantification — only 11.1% of studies report prediction intervals; (3) benchmark standardization — heterogeneous datasets and metrics prevent fair model comparison; (4) real-time deployment — no study addresses sub-5-minute resolution for grid frequency regulation.

### 4.3 Comparison with Previous Reviews

Compared to earlier reviews by Ahmed et al. (2020), Sobri et al. (2018), and Raza et al. (2020), this SLR reveals several evolving trends. First, the proportion of DL-based studies has increased from approximately 30% (pre-2020) to 55.6% (2021-2025). Second, attention mechanisms and Transformers — absent from pre-2020 reviews — now represent the cutting edge. Third, the hybrid model paradigm has matured from simple CNN-LSTM concatenation to sophisticated attention-weighted architectures. Fourth, the persistent underrepresentation of developing regions noted by Sobri et al. (2018) remains unresolved, suggesting systemic barriers to data accessibility and research funding.

### 4.4 Implications for Grid Operators and Policymakers

For grid operators, the findings suggest that: (a) hybrid CNN-LSTM models offer the best cost-accuracy tradeoff for intra-day dispatch planning; (b) Transformer architectures should be considered for day-ahead unit commitment when ≥2 years of training data are available; (c) ensemble approaches combining 3-5 base models provide robust worst-case performance during extreme weather events. For policymakers, the geographic imbalance necessitates funding for open-source PV datasets in underrepresented climate zones. Standardized benchmarking frameworks aligned with IEA Task 16 recommendations would accelerate model intercomparison and technology transfer.

### 4.5 Limitations of This Review

Several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the search was restricted to three databases (Scopus, IEEE Xplore, ScienceDirect) and English-language publications, potentially excluding relevant studies indexed elsewhere. Second, the 18-study sample, while adequate for qualitative synthesis, precludes meta-analytic pooling due to heterogeneous metrics and datasets. Third, publication bias favoring positive results may overstate model performance. Fourth, the rapid pace of DL innovation means architectures published after May 2025 are not captured.

### 4.6 Future Research Directions

Based on the identified gaps, we propose six priority research directions: (1) Transfer learning frameworks enabling model generalization across climate zones with minimal local retraining; (2) Probabilistic forecasting with conformal prediction intervals for risk-aware grid management; (3) Multi-modal fusion integrating sky cameras, satellite imagery, and NWP outputs; (4) Standardized benchmark suites with uniform datasets, metrics, and baseline models; (5) Federated learning architectures enabling collaborative model training without sharing proprietary PV data; (6) Edge-deployable lightweight models for real-time inverter-level forecasting at sub-minute resolution.

### 4.7 Synthesis and Contributions

This SLR contributes to the literature by: (a) providing the first PRISMA-guided systematic synthesis of ML/DL solar PV forecasting research for 2021-2025; (b) quantitatively characterizing model performance across architectures, horizons, and climates; (c) identifying actionable research gaps with specific methodological recommendations; and (d) proposing a benchmarking framework aligned with IEA guidelines. The synthesis confirms that while ML/DL methods have matured significantly, the field faces a critical transition from proof-of-concept single-site studies to robust, generalizable, and uncertainty-aware forecasting systems suitable for global deployment.
